item.title: Exclusive: Anthropic's plan to protect critical infrastructure
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 1.14
Anthropic is launching a new cybersecurity initiative designed to bring its most powerful AI models and engineers to companies protecting power grids, water utilities and other critical infrastructure, the company first shared with Axios. Why it matters: Critical infrastructure operators are struggling to secure aging, complex systems as AI threatens to make cyberattacks faster and cheaper to execute. Driving the news: Under its new Critical Infrastructure Defense Program, Anthropic will provide its frontier AI models, onsite engineers and threat research to companies already responsible for securing critical infrastructure systems. Participating companies will use these resources to identify and fix vulnerabilities in their customers' systems. The program's founding partners include Accenture, Booz Allen Hamilton, CrowdStrike, Deloitte, Dragos, Hitachi, Insane Cyber, Nozomi Networks, Palo Alto Networks, PwC and Rockwell Automation. Anthropic said several partners are already using Claude to fix vulnerabilities and help customers do the same. Zoom in: Anthropic is also launching a free AI-powered vulnerability scanning service for open-source software projects, called OSS Scanner. Participating projects will receive periodic scans from Claude, along with automated reports detailing vulnerabilities, how they could be exploited and suggested fixes. The reports won't undergo human review before being sent to software maintainers, meaning some findings could be inaccurate. The big picture: Anthropic, OpenAI and other AI developers are looking for ways to put their most powerful models in the hands of cyber defenders as hackers gain access to similar capabilities . Anthropic's new initiative builds on lessons from Project Glasswing, which gave vetted organizations access to its most capable AI models to identify security vulnerabilities. The company said the project demonstrated how quickly AI can uncover vulnerabilities, but also how difficult it remains to verify and fix them. Yes, but: It's unclear how participating companies will safely test and deploy fixes without disrupting utilities' operations, one of the biggest challenges in securing critical infrastructure. Anthropic also didn't specify whether partners will receive free model access or who will cover the computing costs associated with using its AI tools. Go deeper : AI is supercharging hacks of everyday utilities

item.title: OpenAI's math breakthrough points beyond math
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 1.14
AI's conquest of computer programming offered an early demonstration of what happens when models become good enough at a specialized field that experts can no longer treat them as a novelty. Mathematics appears to be next. Why it matters: OpenAI's latest mathematical results — which involved releasing hundreds of new proofs generated by a powerful, unreleased model — demonstrate that the startling advances of AI are likely to continue moving across entirely new fields. Catch up quick: OpenAI on Tuesday released 722 manuscripts organized into 372 groups of findings (" families ") on long-standing mathematical problems, inviting academics and researchers to examine and build on the material. The reception has mixed scientific excitement with genuine unease. One Rutgers University mathematician said on X that a result connected to the Riemann hypothesis would warrant an automatic Fields Medal if a human had done the work. Some mathematicians have questioned these results, as well as another solution OpenAI released last month , asking whether they represent original breakthroughs or draw heavily from previous human input. Others downplayed the utility of AI-generated math. "You can discover new math easily," Stephen Wolfram, a renowned computer scientist and physicist who has followed AI closely for years, said at a Tuesday event for the National Museum of Mathematics. "You can make a trillion theorems easily. The problem is most of those theorems are not ones that anybody will care about." Zoom in: Like computer programming, mathematics gives AI something unusually valuable: a way to tell when it is right. A proof can be scrutinized by mathematicians and, increasingly, translated into formal languages that computers can verify line by line. Similarly, it is immediately possible to know whether autonomously written AI code actually works. The big picture: Software engineers have already lived through this transition. AI coding tools progressed from autocomplete and debugging to agents capable of writing substantial amounts of software and carrying out complex engineering tasks. The shift has changed not only how code gets written, but what it means to be a programmer, bringing a fair dose of awe, amazement and dread to many lifelong software engineers. Much as software engineers did before them, mathematicians have begun to question the implications of some of the OpenAI discoveries on graduate work, and on training a new generation of theorists. Yes, but: Some software engineers have successfully mapped out the roles humans still play in generating quality products. While new AI coding tools have dramatically increased the code one engineer can ship, humans still play a crucial role in building quality software. Mathematicians have begun to echo that point, noting that the most meaningful advances in their field often involve building a framework or bringing structure to a complex idea. Many are skeptical about whether any AI system will be able to replicate human originality. Between the lines: Beyond mathematics, the results do point to the likelihood that AI disruption will continue moving into new areas, partially answering a long-standing question from AI skeptics. While researchers at rival startups questioned the utility of OpenAI's mathematical findings because of limited practical applications, some acknowledged that they provide evidence of AI's rapid advances.

item.title: Christa Pike left the hospital and returned to Tennessee prison after failed lethal injection
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
Tennessee inmate Christa Pike was released from the hospital and is back in prison more than a week after she survived the state's attempt to execute her by lethal injection , her attorneys said Saturday. The big picture: The failed execution was unprecedented. Pike, 50, got two doses of the deadly drug pentobarbital on Sept. 30 and was still breathing. The state called an ambulance and Pike got life-saving care at a local hospital. Pike's attorneys said they believed she was "brain dead" and on life support. It shocked them and her doctors when she woke up and began talking earlier this week . What they're saying: Pike's attorneys said she had returned to Debra K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center, where she had been housed for decades. "She is grateful to the first responders and her medical team for their care in these extraordinary circumstances," the attorneys said in a statement. "She is continuing to receive medical care at the prison, and we will continue to track her recovery." Catch up quick: Gov. Bill Lee ordered an independent review to determine how Pike was able to survive the attempted lethal injection. Another execution set for December was called off while that investigation plays out. Pike was sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer.

item.title: AI vs. the rest of the economy
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
Data: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, FactSet; Chart: Axios/Matt Phillips; Note: Data center construction includes construction costs, such as labor, materials, profits of contractors, architectural and engineering work and miscellaneous overhead, interest and taxes. Does not include servers, racks, chips or memory. More and more, it seems as if there's the AI economy — and everything else. Why it matters: The growing chasm between the breakneck growth of the AI world and the slower pace of the economy where most Americans work and live has huge implications, especially for the markets. Zoom in: The most recent numbers on U.S. construction spending through August — shown above — paint the picture remarkably clearly. Zoom out: The same divide is an important theme in the markets as well. In corporate bonds, AI-related offerings accounted for more than half of net investment grade issuance for the year through the end of August, according to data from Apollo and Bloomberg. Data: Apollo, Bloomberg; Chart: Axios/Matt Phillips And of course, excitement over all things related to AI has supercharged the market values of Nvidia, the hyperscalers and other AI-related tech stocks. Stunning stat: The weighting of the S&P 500 technology sector in terms of market capitalization is now roughly 40%. That's higher than during the peak of the dot-com bubble. But that actually underplays the impact of AI. If you throw in the hyperscalers Meta and Amazon, which S&P doesn't include in the tech sector, the share of the AI-pilled part of the blue-chip index climbs closer to 50%. Data: FactSet, Axios; Chart: Axios/Matt Phillips The bottom line: The growth gap between AI and everything else means the U.S. economy and the markets are increasingly yoked to AI — and all the risks that come with it.

item.title: SDSU opens lab in Mission Valley for the study of sustainable water management
item.description:
Source: NBC 7 San Diego Pre-analysis score: 0.84
San Diego State University Friday opened the One Water Laboratory, a modular building and outdoor space where students, faculty and community members will collaborate to address some of the region’s most pressing water challenges. The 480-square-foot building along the San Diego River at SDSU Mission Valley will have three central purposes: advancing research on innovative water systems and technologies; expanding education, public engagement and lifelong learning; and providing hands-on training in emerging technologies and fields, such as watershed science and hydrology. “San Diego knows firsthand that drought, water pollution and extreme weather are not abstract concerns,” said SDSU President Adela de la Torre. “At the One Water Lab, our faculty and students can move research beyond theory — testing ideas and technologies in the living watershed and turning knowledge into solutions that protect our water and strengthen our region.” According to the university, the OWL will build on established water research at SDSU across disciplines such as water quality and quantity, flooding and hydrology, remote sensing, wastewater treatment and resource recovery, microbiology, emerging contaminants and the effects of disturbances such as wildfire on watersheds. “One of the most exciting things about the One Water Lab is its potential to bring people together,” said Natalie Mladenov, director of the Water Innovation and Reuse Lab and civil, construction and environmental engineering professor at SDSU. “Our faculty are studying water from so many different perspectives. This facility creates opportunities for those areas of expertise to intersect in new ways.” The OWL is funded in part by $2.6 million in grant funding from the San Diego River Conservancy, an independent agency “established to preserve, restore and enhance the San Diego River Area.” The lab will include signage in honor of Deanna Spehn, who helped create the San Diego River Conservancy and championed its efforts to protect San Diego’s natural resources. Spehn died in 2022. “The plaque honoring Deanna Sphen recognizes her contributions and the spirit of partnership that has made the One Water Lab possible,” said Ben Clay, chair of the San Diego River Conservancy. “The San Diego River Conservancy and SDSU share a longstanding relationship grounded in a commitment to environmental stewardship. We are proud to build on that partnership through a facility that will serve students, researchers and the broader community for years to come.” The lab’s outdoor space includes bioretention basins located throughout the river park. According to the university, the basins were designed to actively capture and filter stormwater runoff from the surrounding landscape, cleaning it before it flows into the San Diego River and makes its way to the Pacific Ocean. “The One Water Lab is SDSU Mission Valley’s first dedicated research facility, but it represents only the beginning of what has long been planned for this site,” said Hala Madanat, SDSU vice president for research and innovation. “As the Innovation District continues to take shape, it will create new opportunities for research, education and collaboration that bring together our university, industry and community partners with real-world impact on our region and the world.” OWL’s mission is to recognize “surface water, stormwater and wastewater as essential, interconnected resources for mitigating water scarcity, strengthening climate resilience and sustaining critical ecosystems,” an SDSU statement read. The lab will also host educational opportunities for local K-12 schools, community members and regional partners.

item.title: Politically Speaking: Councilmember Henry Foster's strong feelings on strong mayor
item.description:
Source: NBC 7 San Diego Pre-analysis score: 0.84
Councilmember Henry Foster is fighting for his seat on San Diego’s City Council in a nail-biter race. The District 4 representative stands firm in his votes over his tenure on the council so far, and has some strong feelings about the strong mayor form of government. He sat down with NBC 7 Political Reporter Joey Safchik on Politically Speaking this week. A transcript of the interview is below. Safchik: On the San Diego City Council. An incumbent is defending his seat, and a challenger appears to be putting up quite the offensive fight. Today we’re looking at district four, including Encanto, Mountain View and Paradise Hills. Council member Henry Foster hopes to continue speaking for those communities. He’s here with me now to tell us why he should. Thank you for being here. Foster: Oh my pleasure. Happy to be here. Safchik: Why do you think this race has gotten so heated? It came down to 12 votes between you in the primary. Foster: Well, I think it’s just an indication of what’s taking place at the federal level with our current president and folks just being frustrated, frustrated on the cost of living, frustrated on gas prices. And just, frustrated, not being heard. And so, I think competition is good. And I think there’s an opportunity, and just an opportunity, opportunity to further engage with the community. Safchik: You feel like they’re taking out their frustrations with those federal policies on you, perhaps? Foster: I wouldn’t say that they’re taking it out on me. I think they’re just engaging. And I think they are looking to make sure their voices are heard, and I think it’s a positive thing. I think competition is good. I’m hoping to see an increase in the numbers of engagement. I believe during the primary, we were roughly around 20,000 voters that engaged. But I’m hoping to see a substantial increase in that number. I think it’s important. I think the midterms are, the election cycle at the federal level is important. I think what we have going on at the state is important. And of course, at the local level, I think it is very, very important. Safchik: What has this steep competition pushed you to evaluate about yourself and your positions? Foster: I think it’s just a matter of making sure that I’m doing everything I can in regards to voter contact to make sure that everyone understands and is informed. I think there’s a lot of misinformation out there. I think there’s been efforts to intentionally misinform my community. I think there’s a lot of outside forces that have come in to help with that misinformation. And I’m just there to meet with my neighbors, to fellowship with my neighbors and to make sure they have a clear understanding. Safchik: What have you accomplished over the last two years in this seat that you think should give voters confidence that they should reelect you? Foster: Well, I think that’s an excellent question. One, I think I am bringing a level of accountability and transparency to city government that I think, has not been seen to this level. I think it shows every day. On how I approached my job on the dias. I am very, very pointed with my line of questioning. I am looking to see where we can make improvements in deploying our core services, because that’s what’s important to our community to make sure our infrastructure is being taken care of. And to make sure things like the 2024 floods do not happen again. But when you talk about the accomplishments, one, we all need to understand we’ve been in a budget deficit for decades. But with a budget deficit, I’ve been able to make some significant improvements within the community. One, that I’m very proud of, was bringing the Oak Park library, the new Oak Park Library, to construction. Also, proud to say that, that’s a $37 million project. Doing a deficit, able to make sure that we had 100%, construction funding. I think that speaks to my expertise and my dedication. Also, we have a very significant project that’s going to be happening on Streamview Drive. I think if you go back in time, there were some stories where we had vehicles that were actually becoming projectiles on that block. And so we have a $64 million project that is going to, improve, Streamview Drive and bring some important infrastructure, some green infrastructure and some public safety improvements. So I think that’s very significant. And also just what we’ve been able to do in the black arts and culture district. One thing that we have done, I am so proud to say that we brought back, what I want to say, a legacy event. And that was the Encanto Street Fair. We have rebranded the Encanto Block Party and Music Festival, and we had about 1500 residents out, enjoying the community fellowship in, in the district. And I think that’s what I’m looking to see happen. Within our community, that fellowship, that level of love and attention, throughout the district. Safchik: There are some folks who say the city government should be taking care of homelessness and infrastructure and housing. Why did you feel that library project and arts and culture funding were priorities in your district? Foster: Well, because I think if you look at what has been on the table as we’ve been going through the structural deficit, one area that seems to be a point of contention is immediately cutting our libraries, our park and rec hours. For me, we live in a community that needs every opportunity for our young people to have a safe place, a place where they could go, do their homework, learn, and focus on their education. Yes, streets, roads, infrastructure, homeless are important, but we also need to make sure that we are doing everything we can to invest in our youth to make sure that they have every opportunity. One thing I said when I ran for this office is that I want to make sure, as I grew up in district four, as I have been able to reach the level of success that I have been able to achieve. I want to make sure every family, every young person has that same opportunity that I have. Safchik: How would you describe your reputation as a council member? Foster: I think, firm but fair, I think is a very, very, simple characterization. I love my community. I know my community. When I was a young boy, I made my way throughout the community by walking. Riding a bike or a skateboard. And so, back when I was coming up, not too many places you can go where neighbors didn’t know you were neighbors. Make sure you did what you were supposed to do and stayed away from those things that you were not to be involved in. And so for me, I think that’s critical. And, everything I do every day, every day, I start with one question, and that’s what’s in the best interest of district four. And as I do my analysis, my due diligence and work with the team and the community, I also end with that same question. What’s in the best interests of district four? Safchik: We’ve talked about what you’re proudest of. Looking back at the last two years, what, if anything, would you have done differently? Foster: I think that I would have made sure that the understanding of a strong mayor form of government is fully understood. And what implications? Those have to be a community like District 4. Oftentimes I get asked, why are we not seeing the investment? And I think that’s a direct question on our budget. I think our budget is a symbol or a representation of our morals and values. And so I think, really, having more dialogue about our budget, how the budget works, where the investment is going. I think it is something that I will further highlight to the community. So, for example, typically we always go out and we bring the IBA out and we go through a budget town hall. I think we need to increase the amount of those town halls instead of having one. Maybe we do it from a regional approach within the community. We have 18 communities, and I think we need to make sure that we touch each of those communities to make sure, again, that residents feel that they are heard. And there’s a clear understanding on what’s being presented and what those potential outcomes can be. Safchik: During a meeting a few weeks ago, you floated the idea of a ballot measure to do away with the strong mayor form of government. If you’re reelected, will you be pushing for that? Foster: Well, again, I think it’s dependent upon the decisions that the mayor makes. I think one thing that I think. Safchik: So is it a gripe with this particular mayor or with the system as a whole? Foster: I think it’s the system as a whole. Right now, we do not have what I would term a professional chief operating officer, someone that has the expertise, the experience that can deal with the complexities of a large organization such as the city of San Diego. And I think based on our current policies, procedures, our charter, our municipal code. I think there’s some work we need to do to make sure that we codify that the COO position is important and that it should be maintained and that it should be a field position. So the people understand that they have someone that understands all the complexities of the city of San Diego and delivers our core services accordingly. Safchik: Would you consider yourself one of the chief critics of Mayor Gloria? Foster: Absolutely. Again, I would like to say I do what I do on behalf of the residents of my community. If someone wants to understand when their street will be paved, I think that’s a very reasonable question. And we should be able to provide an accurate and reasonable response when people are concerned about El Nino. I think that the operations staff should be out in the community, working with the community, preparing the community. In regards to the expected rainfall and the potential damages that are coming. And so I think we just need to do more. I think it needs to be forward facing, and I think we need to meet those obligations with our residents. Safchik: Voice of San Diego is reporting that the mayor has been pushing interest groups to drop or reconsider their support of you. Why do you think he would be doing that? Foster: I think it’s because of the accountability that I bring to the table. I’ve been one of the most vocal council members on the dais. I’m going to continue to be vocal because I take my job very seriously. And I think, when I took my oath, I have an obligation to my community, to my neighbors, and I’m going to put my best foot forward to make sure that I am doing everything I can do to make sure that our decisions are based from an equity perspective and that, we are addressing the deficiencies throughout my community, just as we are addressing deficiencies in all the other communities throughout the city of San Diego. Safchik: The firefighters union dropped their endorsement of you. What do you attribute that to? Foster: I think it’s just a bad decision. I think Local 145, their executive board, I think they just need to come to the table, have a conversation. I think their decision was a mistake. And I think that’s a question for 145, because I have had no dialogue with them. We just simply received an email, and that was it. Safchik: Does it make you reconsider any of your positions? Foster: Absolutely not. Again, I’m here to serve the residents of District 4. Every decision I make starts with what’s in the best interests of District 4. And every decision ends with what’s in the best interest of District 4. And I’m going to continue to do that. No matter where this support comes from or where the support does not come from. Safchik: Your communities, like you’ve talked about extensively already, were hardest hit by the floods back in 2024. What have you done to fortify these neighborhoods? Should there be any extreme weather from this El Nino potential? El Nino? Foster: That’s a very good question. One thing that I have done since I’ve been in office is to prioritize the families that have been impacted by the floods. We understand the areas that are most vulnerable. And my team has been out monitoring all of the progress within our current channels and creeks. We are making sure that they are being maintained, maintained appropriately. Also in this last budget cycle, I am proud to say that we were able to, at the request of our fire chief, Chief Logan, we were able to allocate an additional $2 million in El Nino preparation to make sure that we were supporting our fire chief and our emergency department. And so we’re going to keep doing that. Also, I’ve been adamant and I’ve been advocating and working on our [low interest federal] loans. We have over $190 million in low interest federal loans that are specifically for District 4 to address the various channels and creeks that we have throughout our area. So we are in full design mode in several areas. One of the areas that we are reaching full design completion is in the area of Encanto at Marie Widman Park. So we are going to see some significant things moving there. Some significant work with our infrastructure. And so I’m looking for that work to continue. I’m going to continue to prioritize and monitor, to monitor the progress, to make sure we get it done timely and as efficiently as we can. Safchik: How confident can people in your district be that they’re going to be safe, that their property is going to be safe this winter? Foster: Well, I think again, that’s why I say we need to communicate. We need to show the community that we are here for them, that we have, they have our full support in the city of San Diego is going to do everything we can to prevent the disaster that we saw in 2024. Safchik: Has that progress moved fast enough to protect people? Foster: Let me say this: it has not moved fast enough to my liking. Safchik: You feel you’ve done everything you can? Foster: I have done everything I can. Again, we are in a strong mayor form of government. The mayor determines who shows up on what day, what time and what location. I’m going to continue to push. I’m going to continue to make sure that district four is prioritized. And that’s the passion you see on the dias. That’s the passion you’re going to continue to see. Safchik: What more would you ask of the mayor than when it comes to your community and stormwater? Foster: Simply get it done. That’s it. Get it done, get it done. Safchik: You have been a vocal opponent of Flock since the get go. If you were reelected, what more would you do to push Flock out of San Diego? Foster: I think I will come to someone like you, ask you to get on board. I ask you to help push that message because I think it’s a clear message, a message of overreach. I think if you look at that contract, if you look at what took place, I think there’s some very, very significant ethical concerns that need to be addressed. We had an officer that was employed at the city of San Diego that we went into an exclusive negotiating contract, and now that officer has retired and works for Flock. I would ask NBC to carry that story. I would ask NBC to do the due diligence and do some investigative reporting and bring that information to light. And let’s do what’s right by the people of the city of San Diego, and let’s get Flock out of this city. Safchik: Our job absolutely is to share the facts. And obviously this is a platform for you to express your opinion legislatively. Is there anything more you’d like to see done legislatively? Foster: We have put everything in place that we have the authority to do. Safchik: Do you feel like your hands are tied now? Foster: Absolutely. I think this again, this becomes the decision of the mayor and the nine. Where do we stand? What type of San Diego do we want to be? And I think that is a decision that each person in this city needs to engage in and needs to come to the table and cast their vote. That’s why voting is so important, and that’s why representation is important. Because flock has been known to create privacy issues. There’s officers that misuse and abuse the system. I think that’s very well documented, not only in the city of San Diego, but throughout the nation. And this mass surveillance needs to stop. Safchik: If you are reelected, what are you going to do to make life more affordable or housing more accessible for your constituents? Foster: Well, I think in the area of housing, one thing that we need to make sure that we do is that we make sure that we are doing everything we can to be in conformance with the Baker versus the city of San Diego settlement. And that settlement indicates that we should be focusing our affordable housing in high to highest resource areas. I think that’s step number one. Making sure that we are making those opportunities available. Also, part of that settlement, there’s $500,000 that was to be allocated to first time homebuyer programs. I think we need to make sure that that money gets allocated, that we work with the San Diego Housing Commission and make sure that we are making those types of purchases that access to generational wealth. I think we need to make that a reality. Also, I think we’ve done a good job. I think the state has done a good job at identifying the housing as a crisis, but I think we could do more. I think we need to actually look at how we can utilize our purchasing power. I think we should actually do more to drive the cost of housing down. Right now, I don’t think we have done a good job. Safchik: How do you do that? Why hasn’t it happened already? Foster: Because of the risk. I think there are concerns about risk. I think we should look at the requirements that we make our contractors do when it comes to insurance policies versus contractors pulling their own insurance. I think there’s ways we can do ownership or have the government get involved in the insurance process, and decrease that liability in that cost. I also think we can do what a lot of large contractors have done, and that’s to start working to where we are actively involved in purchasing lumber and purchasing doors and purchasing windows, purchasing building and construction materials to make sure that we are leveraging our volume. It’s almost– the difference of why people go to Costco versus going to a grocery store and buying in bulk. When you buy in bulk, you tend to drive the cost down. And so I think we need to do more with the materials, the building materials, and also with land. I think there are things that we can do with land banking and land trust, to bring those costs down. But we can’t simply just do the status quo. We can’t simply just identify potential land that is open and available for building and leave it to the developers. I think we need to do more to actually impact the cost. Safchik: Are you worried that the Balboa parking debacle, the trash fee saga, those things that made life slightly less affordable for San Diegans, that those are going to haunt your campaign? Foster: No, I do not. Safchik: You stand by your decisions? Foster: Absolutely. One thing that I think folks need to understand. I voted no on trash. That was not a Henry Foster decision. I have fought those costs from day one. Safchik: You had very strong feelings a couple of weeks ago about that error. Foster: Absolutely. With the overcharging that took place in regards to Balboa Park. Again, I’m going to say this. I put the community of district four first. My community does not go to Balboa Park when there’s a birthday party, when there’s a family reunion. We just had one of the oldest families in district four have a family reunion at Neal Petties Park. That’s where my community fellowships. That is what my community calls home. And so for me, that decision put my people first. Safchik: You are hoping the dollars generated from Balboa Park would open up money to go towards your community, those parks. Foster: Absolutely. To keep libraries open, to keep park and rec hours open. That’s important to my community. If you look at Balboa Park, look at the leases in Balboa Park. No one pays for the leases in Balboa Park. No one pays a water bill in Balboa Park. And those are the things that I think if we communicate to the public and we communicate effectively, then there’s more understanding. And people are able to make their decisions from an informed place. Those are the things that we need to clean up. Safchik: I speak to a lot of voters who feel like the city is a bit dysfunctional right now. That is a word I hear over and over again. Do you think that’s a fair characterization? Foster: I think the council is working together to address the residents’ concerns. Again, this is a strong mayor form of government. The mayor is responsible for the condition of our streets, our roads, our stormwater system, our parks, our libraries, our police department, our fire department. And so I think that’s why it’s even much more important to engage, to come to the table. Let your voices be heard. Vote. And let’s make sure we at the end of the day, after November 3rd, let’s roll our sleeves up and continue to get back to work and to serve the residents of the city of San Diego. Safchik: All right. We will leave it at that. Councilmember Foster, thank you so much for being here. Foster: All right. Thank you.

item.title: Silicon Valley's horror shows
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
Hollywood's hottest villain right now is the tech billionaire. Four films hitting theaters this fall put some of Silicon Valley's most powerful and controversial figures in the spotlight: Elon Musk , Mark Zuckerberg, Sam Altman and Elizabeth Holmes. Why it matters: Hollywood's portrayal of Silicon Valley and its leaders is getting darker as negative headlines about the tech industry seep into pop culture. Once portrayed as brilliant but flawed innovators, tech leaders are increasingly being cast as creepy villains whose ambitions may do more harm than good. Zoom in: This fall's tech billionaire films span genres, from documentaries to thrillers. 💻 "The Social Reckoning," Aaron Sorkin's follow-up to his 2010 hit, "The Social Network," opened Friday with Jeremy Strong portraying a more sinister Mark Zuckerberg during the 2021 Facebook whistleblower leak . Sorkin takes some cinematic liberties with chronology and other details. 🚀 "Musk," the four-hour documentary ( including a 10-minute intermission) about Elon Musk's rise, is playing in select theaters and opens nationwide on Friday. The roller-coaster rollout of the film, directed by Oscar-winning documentarian Alex Gibney, included critical acclaim at the Venice Film Festival and legal threats from Musk's team. 🩸 "You Can See Everything," out Friday, is an experimental documentary from Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim that follows ex-Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes in the weeks before she went to prison. The studio, A24, says an "intimate portrait of an enigmatic felon becomes a mind-bending three-year journey into the abyss." ( More on the film .) 🤖 "Artificial," a drama directed by Luca Guadagnino, stars Andrew Garfield as Sam Altman and hits theaters Christmas Day. In the film, "[Garfield] depicts Altman as a manipulative, power-hungry psychopath who lies as easily as he breathes and will use anyone, anytime, anywhere to get what he wants," The Verge reports . The studio, NEON, calls it "the story of OpenAI and a two-decade artificial intelligence arms race. ... As the technology becomes more powerful and more valuable than anyone ever imagined, a battle rages over who should control the tech that could change the fate of humanity." These projects represent a sharp turn away from some earlier movies and documentaries about Silicon Valley, like "Jobs" and "Something Ventured," which celebrated the ingenuity of founders and venture capitalists. "With tech, it was an ardent love affair," says Margaret O'Mara, a University of Washington historian who studies Silicon Valley. "And when you fall out of love, you fall out of love fast." "Our popular understanding of Silicon Valley and the products it makes has changed drastically." Zoom out: Hollywood is reflecting the public's growing disillusionment with the tech industry. Polls show Americans of all ages are quickly souring on AI and think it's moving too fast. Two in three Americans say social media has been bad for democracy, per Pew Research Center polling . "Popular movies hold up a mirror to current social anxieties," says writer and editor-in-chief of Film Quarterly J.M. Tyree. Right now, "people are thinking about power consolidating in the hands of the few at the expense of the many." The intrigue: Tech founders are compelling on-screen villains, Tyree says. They bring together two archetypes: the ruthless businessman who's corrupted by greed, as seen in movies like "Citizen Kane" and "The Wolf of Wall Street," and the mad scientist who's morally ambiguous and employs science and technology recklessly, like in "Metropolis" or "Frankenstein." Plus, their eccentricities make for good entertainment. The bottom line: O'Mara, the Silicon Valley historian, notes: "One thing I have learned from studying the history of rich people is that extreme wealth makes you weird."

item.title: Labor Department marks low layoffs milestone
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
Data: U.S. Department of Labor ; Chart: Courtenay Brown/Axios New applications for unemployment benefits have stayed below 200,000 in a stretch rarely seen in modern history. Jobless claims fell by 2,000, to 197,000, last week, the Labor Department said Thursday morning. Why it matters: It points to a remarkable stability on the "firing" side of the labor market, even amid a slower pace of hiring on the other side of the equation. That is helping to keep unemployment low, but it also masks a growing divide between Americans who have jobs and those struggling to find one. What they're saying: "New jobless claims have been under 200,000 for a month now, an incredibly low level of layoffs for a sustained period of time that hasn't been seen since the 1960s," Navy Federal Credit Union chief economist Heather Long said. By the numbers: The four-week average, which smooths out weekly volatility, fell to 198,000, its lowest level since the red-hot job market of 2022–2023. The other side: Jobless claims don't capture every layoff. Some workers receive severance, don't qualify for benefits or find the application process too cumbersome. Still, when layoffs have surged across the economy, claims have surged with them — including during the recessions after the financial crisis and the pandemic. The absence of such an increase now is hard to dismiss. Other data tells a similar story: Announced job cuts fell 20% from a year earlier in September, according to outplacement firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas. The bottom line: Employers may be reluctant to hire, but they appear just as reluctant to fire — an unusual combination that, for now, keeps the labor market on steady footing.

item.title: The Fed's going to take its time with rate hikes
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
A couple more interest rate hikes are probably on the way. But the Federal Reserve is in no great hurry to deliver them. That's the takeaway from the latest round of communications out of the central bank. Why it matters: It implies that the Fed is not in a full-scale effort to tighten the screws on the economy, but rather a cautious recalibration in light of inflationary pressures and robust growth. With Fed chairman Kevin Warsh declining to offer much in the way of guidance, traders and Fed watchers must look to other communications for clues — and the message has been strikingly consistent across the latest crumbs of information. Driving the news: Speaking Thursday morning in Istanbul , Fed governor Christopher Waller explained, with distinctly non-Warshian detail, what kind of interest rate path he anticipates. "If the economic data continue to come in as expected, I anticipate additional hikes to support a timelier return of inflation to our 2 percent goal," he said. "But there is some flexibility about when those hikes will occur. The hikes do not need to come at consecutive meetings, but they should be in place in an acceptable period of time." That aligns with the language in the minutes of the September policy meeting released Wednesday afternoon, stating that "most participants assessed that another increase in the target range for the federal funds rate would likely be appropriate by year-end," but that they "approached each meeting with an open mind." Of note: The minutes and Waller comments come after fairly explicit comments last week from vice chair Philip Jefferson and New York Fed president John Williams waving away expectations of a second rate increase at a meeting concluding Oct. 28. Zoom in: That doesn't answer the question of how big this tightening cycle will turn out to be. But the tea leaves point to one more rate hike at this year's final meeting and another early in 2027. That would amount to a total of 0.75 percentage point of rate increases, the same size adjustment as easing cycles in 2019 and 2025. Waller, in an extended musing about Fed communication strategy in Thursday morning's speech, used a 0.75-point adjustment as the hypothetical cumulative adjustment. If nothing else, it's a hint that he sees three rate hikes in this adjustment cycle as the most probable course of action. Between the lines: Warsh is determined to maintain optionality and not pre-commit to a policy path, and he still has that. But talk of leaving rates steady in October and keeping the cumulative adjustment modest tells us something about what kind of rate cycle Fed leadership envisions. This is not — in their view, at least — the beginning of a sustained, open-ended tightening cycle needed to slow the economy and break the back of inflation, as last seen in 2022. Rather, it's a take-your-time, limited operation to better calibrate policy for the mix of solid labor market results, accelerating growth and elevated inflation that they see. What they're saying: "With evidence that economic activity is strengthening in the second half of this year, I am not greatly concerned that tighter monetary policy threatens a damaging slowdown in the economy," Waller said Thursday morning. "But I am concerned that the recent acceleration in inflation — after what soon will be five and a half years of it above the FOMC's target — will lead consumers, investors, and price-setting businesses to revise up their expectations for future inflation." The bottom line: Investors can take solace that the Fed is not preparing aggressive action to take away the punchbowl. The open question is whether this limited tightening will do the trick in getting inflation down faster.

item.title: "The Axios Show": Inside Bryan Johnson's quest to make 300 the new 70
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
Bryan Johnson , the face of the longevity movement, wants to make staying alive more important than making money. The famous/infamous biohacker spends over $2 million a year on his health, talks about living forever and publicly tracks everything from his erections to his sperm strength. Why it matters: As Johnson fights to "live forever," he's doing so with a wink to his 8 million social media followers, a link to his business in his bio and a knack for drawing attention to himself. What they're saying: In his interview with The Axios Show, he offered some advice for Elon Musk, said he'd love to help President Trump with his health and revealed his ultimate goal. "Will the 25th century ... be like, 'thank you' in 500 years? Will they give me a head nod? That's the goal," he said. Zoom out: His big picture focus: change the focus of society to health, not wealth. "Society says making money... is the greatest trophy one can get...we are at this inflection moment as a species where we are transitioning to 'Don't Die,'" Johnson said, referring to the title of his longevity movement. "What creates status and power and prestige is going to be different. And as crazy as it sounds, it may be your nighttime erections...It may be your ability to dunk a basketball at age 49," he said. Johnson, 49, is currently trying to dunk . Zoom out: That focus is what drives some of his more extreme experiments and interventions. In 2023, Johnson injected his teenage son's plasma , which he found to be a helpful regimen for his dad but not for himself, saying his own biomarkers are already "pretty similar to my 18-year-old." Through the help of wearables, tests and a concierge team, Johnson has gathered over 4.2 billion data points about his own body and health, and he relies on AI tools to help parse takeaways from that data. He has an in-home medical lab of sorts where he can do continuous testing, monitoring and procedures. Zoom in: Perhaps his most extreme act is his online presence , which Johnson called "performance art" in our conversation. When talking about humans dramatically increasing lifespans through scientific methods, "no one cares," he said. But "if you talk about it in performance art where it has a vibe and an energy to it, people will engage." The intrigue: Still, even Johnson recommends many of the basics for health: sleep, healthy diet and exercise. For those who want to go further, he recommends a blood draw or MRI, sitting in a sauna several times a week and testing out psychedelics. When asked which longevity treatments feel like snake oil, Johnson said "Basically everything on social media." When I pointed out that includes Bryan, he said, "you're right. I've done this for years. Most things don't work." Reality check: Johnson has multiple longevity businesses that he calls successful, though the financials of the companies are not public. Blueprint , his consumer products business, sells "the most tested healthy longevity protocols," per the company: protein powders, supplements and even extra virgin olive oil. Immortals , another one of his companies, offers concierge longevity care for a limited group of members. Prices range from $75,000 a year to $1 million per year. Johnson has "very complicated emotions about this business because I started the company to try to help other people and not to make money. ...I'd rather just be clean and be like, "I'm going to help you out." But to help people out, I have to have infrastructure to actually deliver these things." The intrigue: Johnson said he gets calls from world leaders asking for his advice, and he's in group chats with top tech leaders and influencers. When asked for his health advice for Elon Musk, Johnson said "I hope Elon would clean up his health. I mean, he's worked so hard. He has a lot of potential to enjoy what he's built." The bottom line: Johnson believes wealth is out, health and longevity are in as the new status symbols.

item.title: Data centers face a sweeping new power regime
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
Lawmakers are considering forcing data centers to shoulder new costs and restrictions while speeding up the energy infrastructure needed to power the AI boom. Why it matters: The bipartisan legislation, unveiled last week, represents the most aggressive response yet from Washington to data centers amid growing backlash over their energy and environmental impacts. Driving the news: The provisions are part of broader Senate legislation aimed at speeding up permitting for energy — but make no mistake: The data center measures are significant and would go far beyond Washington's largely voluntary efforts to date. The bill's sponsors say it would accelerate energy development while ensuring data centers pay their share of grid upgrades. "I don't think we've seen it before," said Ari Peskoe, director of the Electricity Law Initiative at Harvard Law School, about the proposed additional costs and restrictions. "But I don't think we've seen growth that's comparable to data centers today, and I certainly don't know any industry whose electricity usage has captured so much political attention." Between the lines: For tech companies, the bill cuts both ways. Congress would make it easier to build the energy infrastructure they need while erecting a sweeping framework aimed at keeping other electricity customers from footing the bill. "Just to be candid, having some teeth on data center accountability and ratepayer protection is just table stakes to getting a deal done," said Jane Flegal, a former White House official under President Biden and now a senior fellow at the nonprofit Searchlight Institute. The big picture: Congress has been talking about overhauling permitting for years. The AI boom has given lawmakers an urgent reason to finally act: America suddenly needs enormous amounts of new power infrastructure, fast. Faster approvals for power plants and transmission lines could directly benefit data centers struggling to secure enough electricity for their expansion. How it works: The bill reaches into virtually every part of the relationship between large data centers and the electric grid. Data centers would be required to pay both their share of the existing transmission network and the incremental transmission costs needed to serve them, reversing a decades-old federal pricing policy that generally prevents charging both. This is the biggie, but it doesn't stop there. New data centers of at least 20 megawatts would have to bear the incremental costs they impose across the power system, including generation, storage, transmission and distribution. Regulators at both the federal and state levels could charge large data centers even more than those incremental costs — and use the excess to reduce other customers' bills. Data centers would remain on the hook for infrastructure costs even if they stop buying electricity before those costs have been recovered. Utilities would also have to secure financial guarantees before building infrastructure to serve them, protecting ratepayers if projects don't materialize. Zoom in: States are already moving aggressively to protect ratepayers, with dozens of policies pending or in place across more than half the states aimed at making data centers shoulder more of the costs of serving them. The bill would explicitly give states wide latitude to go further, including treating data centers less favorably than other large industrial customers, competitively allocating access to electricity and requiring them to secure new power supplies or accept limits on electricity use. What they're saying: Not much publicly, yet. The Data Center Coalition, which represents companies across the industry, said it is still reviewing the legislation. Microsoft, Google and Nvidia declined to comment, while Meta didn't respond to a request for comment. Amazon energy policy director Craig Sundstrom said the aging grid and slow permitting are putting pressure on electricity costs, adding that the bill "could unlock the investment needed to build new generation and transmission faster." The intrigue: One tech industry official called some provisions an "unprecedented level of discriminatory treatment" for a single industry. The official, who spoke anonymously to discuss industry deliberations, said tougher grid-connected requirements could encourage some developers to build more power systems completely off-grid instead — potentially undermining the overarching purpose of the bill. The other side: Travis Fisher, a former Trump White House energy official now at the libertarian Cato Institute, said he has "mild support" for the approach despite concerns about setting a discriminatory precedent. He said the provisions "break new ground" at the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission but are consistent with the White House's ratepayer-protection pledge many of the largest data center companies have already signed . What we're watching: Flegal said she would be "incredibly surprised" if tech companies ultimately oppose the broader package. What's next: With the Senate out of town ahead of the midterm elections, lawmakers and stakeholders have plenty of time to push for changes before a possible lame-duck debate. item.title: Americans' trust in the food safety net is spoiling
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
Data: Gallup; Chart: Avery Lotz/Axios Americans' confidence in the safety of food on grocery store shelves — and in the federal government's ability to regulate it — has plummeted to new lows according to a new Gallup poll. The big picture: Simultaneous illness outbreaks put federal regulators under a microscope earlier this year, as layoffs across the nation's health apparatus were already causing food safety angst. By the numbers: Less than half of U.S. adults have a great deal (11%) or a fair amount (36%) of confidence in the federal government to ensure food safety, according to the poll, which was conducted last month. On the flip side, a majority have not much or no confidence in the government's ability to police their food — a first in Gallup's trend, which has been intermittent for two decades. Zoom out: Meanwhile, Americans' confidence in the food sold at grocery stores has mirrored that drop, falling to a record low of 65% saying they are somewhat or very confident. That share has plunged from the 81% recorded in 2019. Zoom in: That growing food safety suspicion is driven by Democrats and independents, while Republicans have actually become more confident in grocery store food. The partisan chasm over the federal government's ability to ensure food safety has flipped — and widened — under the second Trump administration. In 2024, half of Republicans had a great deal or fair amount of confidence in the government to ensure food safety, while nearly three-quarters of Democrats agreed. By 2025, Democrats' confidence fell to 48%, and to 30% in 2026. Republicans, meanwhile, found new faith, with their confidence climbing from 62% in 2025 to 70% to 2026. Catch up quick: This year's polling occurred during and after the federal government declared the end of an outbreak of Cyclospora, a parasite that caused stomach illnesses, two deaths and saw more than 500 hospitalizations across 21 states. Federal health officials eventually traced the rapidly spreading surge to iceberg lettuce from supplier Taylor Farms . But the food woes didn't stop there: This summer saw a flurry of overlapping recalls and FDA investigations, while health experts warned administration cuts had weakened the public health infrastructure responsible for detecting outbreaks. Meanwhile, significant shares of Americans report concerns or strain about affording those groceries. The food-at-home CPI, for grocery store or supermarket food purchases, was up 2.2% between August 2025 and 2026. Friction point: That collides with an administration that's pushed whole foods as part of its "Make America Healthy Again" campaign under Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. But Gallup's polling indicates Republicans have digested that food safety message far better than Democrats and independents. Go deeper: America's next grocery shock is brewing

item.title: The Scramble for the Open Seas
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Pre-analysis score: 0.84
Over the last half millennium, societies around the globe competed to divide up the world’s land. Nearly every square inch of soil outside Antarctica is now owned and tucked within national borders. But the oceans have largely been spared that fate. There were times throughout history when countries tried to gate and regulate the seas, but they were too vast to be controlled for long periods. During the Cold War, as technology made it far easier to imagine partitioning the world’s waterways and seabeds, great powers avoided an unrestrained race to grab the oceans. Most governments agreed to deal with them through a patchwork of treaties and multilateral bodies that sought to guarantee freedom of navigation in international waters and assign coastal seabeds to adjacent littoral states.
